title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
The page has three short items: two geometric fragments of Euler edited by N. Fuss, and one analytic note credited to Lexell.

(103) Approximate n-section of an angle.
- Setup: unit circle with centre C, B=(1,0), A=(cos θ, sin θ).
- Construction: on AC produced beyond C take a = −k·A with k=(n−2)/(2n−1). On CB take b=(m,0) with m=(n−2)/(n+1). The line ab, continued beyond b, meets the arc at O.
- Claim: arc BO ≈ θ/n. For trisection, k=1/5 and m=1/4.
- First-order check: solving the line–circle intersection gives φ = arc BO ≈ k(1−m)θ/(m+k). Since 1−m = 3/(n+1) and m+k = 3n(n−2)/((n+1)(2n−1)), the ratio is exactly 1/n.
- Third-order check: carrying the expansion one order further gives φ = λθ + θ³[λC + λ³/6] + O(θ⁵), with λ=1/n and C = −k/(2M) + (1+m)k²/(2M²) + mk/M² − 1/6, where M=m+k. Substituting Euler's k and m gives C = −1/(6n²), so λC + λ³/6 = 0 identically in n.
- Consequence: the construction is exact through θ³, with error O(θ⁵). The two-parameter family (k,m) is cut to a single point by the conditions at orders 1 and 3. So Euler's constants are precisely the unique choice of this type that kills the cubic error, which the text does not say.
- Numerical check, n=3: θ=90° gives 29.674° (error 0.33°); θ=60° gives 19.962° (error 0.038°). The error ratio ≈ 8.7, against (1.5)⁵ ≈ 7.6, consistent with fifth-order error.

(104) Ptolemy-type identity on a circle.
- Put points a, p, q, b on an arc at arc-coordinates 0, x, y, z. The claim is sin(ny)·sin(n(z−x)) = sin(nx)·sin(n(z−y)) + sin(nz)·sin(n(y−x)).
- This is the classical three-term sine identity, valid for any n by mere rescaling of the angles.
- With n=1/2 it is exactly Ptolemy's theorem for the cyclic quadrilateral, since chord = 2R·sin(arc/2); Euler does not say this.
- As n→0 it gives Euler's four-collinear-points relation aq·bp = ap·bq + ab·pq. The fragment thus interpolates between the line version and the chord version.

(105) Lexell: criterion for rational roots of a cubic.
- Cardano form: the roots of x³=3fx+2g are p+∛q+∛r and the two conjugate forms.
- Assume ∛q, ∛r = s ± t√−3. Then the roots are p+2s and p−s∓3t, and q, r = u ± v√−3.
- Applying this to x³=3fx+2g gives g ± √(g²−f³) = u ± v√−3. Hence f³−g² = 3v², i.e. (f³−g²)/3 must be a square.
- In modern terms this says the discriminant 108(f³−g²) is a rational square.
- Example: roots 3, 7, −10 of x³−79x+210 give (f³−g²)/3 = (442/9)².
- The next page derives the general formula √((f³−g²)/3) = (a−b)(2a+b)(a+2b)/18, adds a parametrization with f = α²+3β², and ends with the discriminant P²Q²−4Q³−4P³R+18PQR−27R² = □ for the general cubic z³+Pz²+Qz+R=0.
errors: Item 105, overstated sufficiency: the text concludes 'quoties (f³−gg)/3 fuerit quadratum, etiam omnes tres radices fore rationales'. A square discriminant is necessary but not sufficient. Counterexample: x³−3x+1=0 (f=1, g=−1/2) gives (f³−g²)/3 = 1/4, a square, yet its roots 2cos(2π/9), 2cos(4π/9), 2cos(8π/9) are irrational (a cyclic cubic).
Item 105, the gap behind that error: the derivation silently assumes the cube roots of u ± v√−3 lie in Q(√−3), i.e. that s and t are rational. This fails exactly in the cyclic, irreducible case.
Item 105 example: the third root is printed as 'III. x = 10'. Since (x−3)(x−7)(x+10) = x³−79x+210 and x=10 gives 420 ≠ 0, the root must be −10. The depressed cubic also needs roots summing to zero.
Item 103: the construction degenerates for n=2, where k=m=0 and a=b=C, and it is meaningless for n=1. This is not noted in the text.

ideas.what: Ruler construction for approximate n-section of an angle via the points Ca=(n−2)/(2n−1)·AC (on AC produced) and Cb=(n−2)/(n+1)·CB; the parameters make the error O(θ⁵).
ideas.modern_name: approximate angle trisection / n-section construction (high-order asymptotic accuracy)
ideas.usually_credited_to: various approximate trisections (e.g. 19th–20th c. engineering-drawing constructions); no specific credit known for this one
ideas.where_published: Only here (Opera postuma 1862, from Adversaria mathematica T. II p. 26), as far as I know

ideas.what: sin(n·aq)·sin(n·bp) = sin(n·ap)·sin(n·bq) + sin(n·ab)·sin(n·pq) for four points on an arc, for any n; the limit n→0 gives the collinear four-point identity.
ideas.modern_name: Ptolemy relation in trigonometric form (three-term sine identity / Plücker-type relation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ptolemy (n=1/2 case); the collinear limit is known as Euler's four-point theorem
ideas.where_published: The collinear-points identity is, I believe, in Euler's Variae demonstrationes geometriae (E135); unsure

ideas.what: Necessary condition for three rational roots of a cubic: (f³−g²)/3 is a rational square, i.e. the discriminant is a square.
ideas.modern_name: square discriminant of a cubic (Galois group in A3)
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical discriminant theory (Lagrange, Gauss, Galois for the group-theoretic meaning)
ideas.where_published: Adversaria note attributed to Lexell, printed here

missed.claim: Euler's approximate n-section construction is not merely first-order correct. For every n its constants make the cubic error term vanish identically (error O(θ⁵)), and they are the unique such pair in this two-point family. The fragment gives the constants without stating this, so the design principle is implicit and appears unrecorded.
missed.quote: In AC producta capiatur Ca=(n−2)/(2n−1) AC; deinde in radio CB capiatur Cb=(n−2)/(n+1) CB
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a small but genuine instance of Euler designing a geometric approximation by asymptotic matching to two orders. It is of interest to the history of approximate constructions and of mechanical drawing.

missed.claim: The sin(n·) form of the identity puts the collinear four-point relation (n→0) and Ptolemy's theorem (n=1/2) in one family. Euler states only the n→0 limit.
missed.quote: ubi pro n numerum quemcunque accipere licet. Hinc si fuerit n numerus valde parvus, erit aq.bp=ap.bq+ab.pq
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Minor; this is a well-known trigonometric identity.

deep.surprise_reason: Items 104 and 105 are routine, and 105 contains a classical error (necessary taken for sufficient). Item 103's construction has a hidden fifth-order accuracy that the text does not explain. This is a pleasant, verifiable detail but of modest significance.
transcription_corrections: Exemplum: the original prints 'III. x = 10'; mathematically it must be x = −10. This is an error of the original, not of the transcription.
